title: Lifting The Maximally-entangledness Assumption In Robust Self-testing For Synchronous Games
authors: Matthijs Vernooij And Yuming Zhao
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2222 (2026).

Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated [MATH] paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient [MATH]-qubit test.

.
tldr: The paper proves that robust self-testing for synchronous games under symmetric projective maximally entangled strategies implies robust self-testing for all quantum strategies, removing an unphysical assumption.
motivation: Robust self-testing in non-local games is a central tool in device-independent quantum information, but existing proofs for synchronous games often rely on the restrictive and unphysical PME strategy assumption.
method: The authors use tracial von Neumann algebra techniques to upgrade robust self-testing guarantees from the PME-restricted setting to arbitrary strategies for perfect synchronous games.
result: They establish a general lifting theorem and apply it to the Quantum Low Degree Test, obtaining an efficient test with an explicit qubit requirement.
conclusion: This work makes PME-based robust self-testing results physically meaningful and broadens their applicability to device-independent certification and complexity-theoretic self-testing.

title: Escaping The Shadow Of Bell’s Theorem In Network Nonlocality
authors: Maria Ciudad Alañón, Emanuel-Cristian Boghiu, Paolo Abiuso, And Elie Wolfe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2213 (2026).

The possibility of nonclassicality in networks unrelated to Bell’s original eponymous theorem has recently attracted significant interest. Here, we identify a sufficient condition for being “outside the shadow of Bell’s theorem” and introduce a testable criterion capable of certifying the novelty of instances of network-nonclassicality which we call minimal network nonclassicality. We provide examples of minimally network nonclassical correlations realizable in quantum theory as well as examples coming from more exotic operational probabilistic theories. In particular, we apply these concepts to the simplest configuration of the 3-chain scenario (a.k.a. the bilocality scenario) to prove that certain correlations have escaped the shadow of Bell's theorem. While some of the examples herein are unprecedented, we also revisit more familiar examples of network nonclassicality in order to highlight the contrast between our approach versus prior approaches with respect to assessing novelty.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a criterion for certifying network nonclassicality that is genuinely independent of Bell's theorem, called minimal network nonclassicality, and applies it to the bilocality scenario.
motivation: Network nonlocality has attracted interest as a form of nonclassicality distinct from standard Bell nonlocality, but it is often unclear whether examples are truly novel or merely shadows of Bell's theorem.
method: The authors formulate a sufficient condition for escaping the shadow of Bell's theorem and define a testable criterion for minimal network nonclassicality, then analyze examples in the 3-chain/bilocality scenario and compare with prior approaches.
result: They provide examples of minimally network-nonclassical correlations realizable in quantum theory and in more exotic operational probabilistic theories, including correlations in the bilocality scenario proven to escape Bell's shadow.
conclusion: The work offers a systematic way to assess the novelty of network-nonclassical correlations and clarifies which examples represent genuinely network-based nonclassicality beyond Bell nonlocality.

title: Non-stabilizerness And Violations Of Chsh Inequalities
authors: Stefano Cusumano, Lorenzo Campos Venuti, Simone Cepollaro, Immacolata de Simone, Gianluca Esposito, Daniele Iannotti, Barbara Jasser, Jovan Odavić, Michele Viscardi, And Alioscia Hamma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2214 (2026).

We study quantitatively the interplay between entanglement and non-stabilizer resources in violating the CHSH inequalities. We show that, while non-stabilizer resources are necessary, they must have a specific structure, namely they need to be both asymmetric and (surprisingly) [MATH]. We employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify the non-stabilizer resources involved and the probability of violation given the resources. We show how spectral quantities related to the flatness of entanglement spectrum and its relationship with non-local SE affect the CHSH inequality. Finally, we utilize these results – together with tools from representation theory – to construct a systematic way of building ensembles of states with higher probability of violation.

.
tldr: The paper quantitatively analyzes how entanglement and non-stabilizer resources jointly enable violations of CHSH inequalities, showing non-stabilizerness must be asymmetric and have a specific structure.
motivation: Understanding which quantum resources are necessary and sufficient for Bell nonlocality is a central question in quantum information theory, and the role of non-stabilizerness beyond entanglement remains insufficiently characterized.
method: The authors employ stabilizer entropy (SE) to quantify non-stabilizer resources, relate spectral properties of the entanglement spectrum to non-local SE, and use representation theory to construct ensembles of states with enhanced CHSH violation probability.
result: They find that non-stabilizer resources are necessary for CHSH violation but must be both asymmetric and surprisingly constrained in structure; spectral flatness of the entanglement spectrum and non-local SE affect the violation probability.
conclusion: The work clarifies the interplay between entanglement and magic in Bell nonlocality and provides a systematic framework for designing states with higher CHSH violation probability, advancing resource-theoretic understanding of nonlocal correlations.

title: Thermodynamic Cost Of A Periodically Driven Quantum System Beyond The Adiabatic Regime
authors: Haowei Wang And Dazhi Xu Xiaoyun Wang
abstract: Finite-time periodic control of an open quantum system is governed by the competition between nonadiabatic driving and reservoir-induced relaxation. We study this competition in a driven two-level system weakly coupled to a single thermal reservoir. Using a nonadiabatic time-dependent quantum master equation, we construct the periodic steady state and separate the dissipated work per cycle into population and nonadiabatic contributions in the instantaneous energy basis. The cycle work is nonmonotonic in the driving frequencies studied and is dominated near its maximum by the nonadiabatic contribution. Nonmonotonicity persists in the examined coupling, temperature, and transverse-amplitude scans. At low frequencies, the work recovers the inverse-period scaling of slow-driving thermodynamics. At higher frequencies, the nonadiabatic work rate ceases to grow in proportion to the driving frequency, and the accumulated work per cycle decreases. We also find that, at finite speed, the ratio of the upward and downward transition coefficients is not determined by the instantaneous energy gap alone and obtain the leading correction to instantaneous detailed balance through a short-memory expansion. These results identify how nonadiabatic transitions and relaxation jointly set the thermodynamic cost of sustaining a periodic quantum process.
tldr: The paper analyzes the thermodynamic cost of periodically driving an open two-level quantum system, separating dissipated work into population and nonadiabatic contributions beyond the adiabatic regime.
motivation: Finite-time periodic control of open quantum systems involves competition between nonadiabatic driving and reservoir relaxation, which is not fully captured by slow-driving thermodynamics.
method: Using a nonadiabatic time-dependent quantum master equation for a weakly coupled driven two-level system, the authors construct the periodic steady state and decompose the cycle work into population and nonadiabatic contributions in the instantaneous energy basis.
result: The work per cycle is nonmonotonic in driving frequency and dominated near its maximum by the nonadiabatic contribution; at high frequencies the nonadiabatic work rate does not scale linearly with frequency, and instantaneous detailed balance receives leading finite-speed corrections.
conclusion: The results clarify how nonadiabatic transitions and relaxation jointly determine the thermodynamic cost of sustaining a periodic quantum process, extending thermodynamic descriptions beyond the adiabatic regime.

title: Spatial Structure Of Multipartite Entanglement At Measurement Induced Phase Transitions
authors: James Allen And William Witczak-Krempa
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2211 (2026).

We study multiparty entanglement near measurement induced phase transitions (MIPTs), which arise in ensembles of local quantum circuits built with unitaries and measurements. In contrast to equilibrium quantum critical transitions, where entanglement is short-ranged, MIPTs possess long-range k-party genuine multiparty entanglement (GME) characterized by an infinite hierarchy of entanglement exponents for k[MATH]2. First, we represent the average spread of entanglement with "entanglement clusters", and use them to conjecture general exponent relations: 1) classical dominance, 2) monotonicity, 3) subadditivity. We then introduce measure-weighted graphs to construct such clusters in general circuits. Second, we obtain the exact entanglement exponents for a 1d MIPT in a measurement-only circuit that maps to percolation by exploiting non-unitary conformal field theory. The exponents, which we numerically verify, obey the inequalities. We also extend the construction to a 2d MIPT that maps to classical 3d percolation, and numerically find the first entanglement exponents. Our results provide a firm ground to understand the multiparty entanglement of MIPTs, and more general ensembles of quantum circuits.

.
tldr: The paper analyzes the spatial structure and scaling of multiparty entanglement near measurement-induced phase transitions using entanglement clusters, measure-weighted graphs, and percolation/CFT mappings.
motivation: Measurement-induced phase transitions exhibit long-range multiparty entanglement unlike equilibrium critical systems, but the hierarchy of k-party genuine multiparty entanglement exponents and their general structure remain poorly understood.
method: The authors introduce entanglement clusters and measure-weighted graphs to characterize average entanglement spread, conjecture exponent relations, and compute exact exponents for a measurement-only 1d MIPT mapped to percolation via non-unitary CFT, with numerical checks and extension to a 2d MIPT.
result: They obtain exact k-party entanglement exponents for the 1d measurement-only circuit, verify them numerically, show they obey classical dominance, monotonicity, and subadditivity inequalities, and numerically extract the first exponents for a 2d MIPT mapping to 3d classical percolation.
conclusion: The results establish a firm structural understanding of multiparty entanglement in MIPTs and provide a framework likely applicable to broader ensembles of quantum circuits.

title: Scalable Long-distance Quantum Fan-out Gates With Reduced Resource Overhead
authors: Wen-Qiang Liu And Hai-Rui Wei
abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an -qubit fan-out gate (also known as a controlled-NOT- -NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared -qubit Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state, local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected -photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.
tldr: The paper proposes an efficient protocol for long-distance n-qubit fan-out gates using a pre-shared GHZ state, local CNOTs, and feed-forward operations, with optical heralded and post-selected implementations.
motivation: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are needed for distributed quantum computation and quantum networks, but standard decomposition-based approaches incur high resource overhead.
method: The protocol uses an n-qubit GHZ state, local CNOT gates, and feed-forward operations; two optical architectures are developed for heralded and post-selected n-photon fan-out gates.
result: The scheme reduces CNOT and Hadamard gate counts and single-photon resource requirements while achieving higher success probabilities than decomposition-based counterparts.
conclusion: The approach is experimentally feasible and represents a practical step toward long-distance quantum computation and scalable quantum networks.

title: Strict Hierarchy Between $n$-wise Measurement Simulability, Compatibility Structures, And Multi-copy Compatibility
authors: Lucas Tendick, Costantino Budroni, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2231 (2026).

The incompatibility of quantum measurements, i.e. the fact that certain observable quantities cannot be measured jointly is widely regarded as a distinctive quantum feature with important implications for the foundations and the applications of quantum information theory. While the standard incompatibility of multiple measurements has been the focus of attention since the inception of quantum theory, its generalizations, such as measurement simulability, [MATH]-wise incompatibility, and mulit-copy incompatibility have only been proposed recently. Here, we point out that all these generalizations are differing notions of the question of how many measurements are genuinely contained in a measurement device. We then show, that all notions do differ not only in their operational meaning but also mathematically in the set of measurement assemblages they describe. We then fully resolve the relations between these different generalizations, by showing a strict hierarchy between these notions. Hence, we provide a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility. Finally, we consider the implications our results have for recent works using these different notions.

.
tldr: The paper establishes a strict hierarchy among generalized notions of measurement incompatibility, including n-wise measurement simulability, compatibility structures, and multi-copy compatibility.
motivation: Generalizations of measurement incompatibility have recently been proposed, but their operational and mathematical relationships were unclear; the authors aim to unify and distinguish these notions.
method: They compare the sets of measurement assemblages described by simulability, n-wise incompatibility, and multi-copy incompatibility, and prove strict inclusions establishing a hierarchy.
result: All considered generalizations are shown to be mathematically distinct, forming a strict hierarchy that clarifies how many measurements are genuinely contained in a device.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for generalized measurement incompatibility and clarifies implications for prior and future results using these notions.

title: Composable Logical Gate Error In Approximate Quantum Error Correction: Reexamining Gate Implementations In Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Codes
authors: Lukas Brenner, Beatriz Dias, And Robert Koenig
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2230 (2026).

Quantifying the accuracy of logical gates is paramount in approximate error correction, where perfect implementations are often unachievable with the available set of physical operations. To this end, we introduce a single scalar quantity we call the (composable) logical gate error. It captures both the deviation of the logical action from the desired target gate as well as leakage out of the code space. It is subadditive under successive application of gates, providing a simple means for analyzing circuits. We show how to bound the composable logical gate error in terms of matrix elements of physical unitaries between (approximate) logical computational basis states. In the continuous-variable context, this sidesteps the need for computing energy-bounded norms. As an example, we study the composable logical gate error for linear optics implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. We find that the logical gate error for implementations of Paulis depends linearly on the squeezing parameter. This implies that their accuracy improves monotonically with the amount of squeezing. For some Cliffords, however, linear optics implementations which are exact for ideal GKP codes fail in the approximate case: they have a constant logical gate error even in the limit of infinite squeezing. This is consistent with previous results about the limitations of certain gate implementations for approximate GKP codes. It shows that findings applicable to ideal GKP codes do not always translate to the realm of physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a composable logical gate error metric for approximate quantum error correction and analyzes linear-optical gate implementations in approximate GKP codes.
motivation: In approximate error correction, logical gates cannot be perfect, so a reliable scalar measure is needed to quantify both deviation from the target gate and leakage out of the code space, especially for continuous-variable GKP codes.
method: The authors define a composable logical gate error that is subadditive under gate composition and bound it using matrix elements of physical unitaries between approximate logical computational basis states, avoiding energy-bounded norms in the continuous-variable setting.
result: For linear-optical implementations of Paulis and Cliffords in approximate GKP codes, Pauli gate error scales linearly with squeezing and improves monotonically, while some Clifford implementations that are exact for ideal GKP codes have constant nonzero error even at infinite squeezing.
conclusion: The composable logical gate error provides a practical circuit-level accuracy measure, and results for ideal GKP codes do not always transfer to physically realizable approximate GKP codes.

title: Fast Bosonic Control Via Multiphoton Qubit-Oscillator Interactions
authors: Noah Gorgichuk, Mohammad Ayyash, Matteo Mariantoni, And Sahel Ashhab
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2224 (2026).

We study the problem of [MATH]-fold rotationally symmetric bosonic state preparation, which is of great importance to bosonic quantum error correction, using a multiphoton interaction between an oscillator and an auxiliary qubit. We present an [MATH]-photon Law-Eberly ([MATH]LE) protocol that serves as an analytic baseline, alongside numerical optimal control calculations that further reduce state preparation time. We find that multiphoton control protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords compared to schemes relying on standard linear interactions. Further, we achieve arbitrary control over the oscillator's Hilbert space by combining different multiphoton interaction orders. We also extend these control improvements to the preparation of rotationally symmetric multi-oscillator states. Lastly, numerical simulations using realistic planar superconducting circuit parameters validate the robustness of our scheme against qubit and oscillator decoherence. Our findings can significantly enhance the performance of bosonic codes on planar superconducting hardware, an important ingredient for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper presents multiphoton qubit-oscillator control protocols that speed up preparation of rotationally symmetric bosonic code states for quantum error correction.
motivation: Bosonic quantum error correction requires fast and robust preparation of nonclassical oscillator states, but standard linear qubit-oscillator interactions are relatively slow.
method: The authors introduce an N-photon Law-Eberly analytic protocol and numerical optimal control using multiphoton interactions between an oscillator and an auxiliary qubit, extending the approach to multi-oscillator states and validating it with realistic superconducting circuit parameters.
result: Multiphoton protocols substantially reduce preparation times for binomial, cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill codewords, enable arbitrary control of the oscillator Hilbert space by combining different interaction orders, and remain robust against qubit and oscillator decoherence.
conclusion: The scheme can enhance bosonic-code performance on planar superconducting hardware and is relevant for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Quantum Graph Theory By Example
authors: Gian Luca Spitzer And Ion Nechita
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2228 (2026).

Quantum graphs have been introduced by Duan, Severini, and Winter to describe the zero-error behaviour of quantum channels. Since then, quantum graph theory has become a field of study in its own right. A substantial source of difficulty in working with quantum graphs compared to classical graphs stems from the fact that they are no longer discrete objects. This makes it generally difficult to construct insightful, non-trivial examples. We present a collection of non-trivial quantum graphs that can be thought of in discrete terms, and that can be expressed in the diagrammatic formalism introduced by Musto, Reutter, and Verdon. The examples arise as the quantum graphs acted on by increasingly smaller classical matrix groups, and are parametrised by triples of matrices [MATH]. The parametrisation reveals a clean decomposition of quantum graph structure into classical and genuinely quantum components: [MATH] and [MATH] are described by a classical weighted graph called the strange graph, while [MATH] provides a purely quantum contribution with no classical analogue. Based on this model, we give exact formulas or establish bounds for quantum graph parameters, such as the number of connected components, the chromatic number, the independence number, and the clique number. Our results provide the first large, parametric families of quantum graphs for which standard graph parameters can be computed analytically.

.
tldr: The paper constructs large parametric families of non-trivial quantum graphs and analytically computes standard graph parameters for them.
motivation: Quantum graphs describe zero-error behavior of quantum channels but are difficult to work with because they are not discrete objects and insightful examples are scarce.
method: The authors use diagrammatic formalism and parametrize quantum graphs via triples of matrices arising from classical matrix group actions, decomposing their structure into classical strange-graph data and a purely quantum component.
result: They obtain exact formulas or bounds for quantum graph parameters including connected components, chromatic number, independence number, and clique number, giving the first large parametric families with analytically computable parameters.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable example-based framework for quantum graph theory and clarifies the split between classical and genuinely quantum graph structure.

title: Unitary Causal Decompositions: A Characterisation Via Lattice Theory
authors: Tein van der Lugt And Robin Lorenz
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2218 (2026).

If a unitary transformation has a circuit representation with no directed path from input [MATH] to output [MATH], then [MATH] does not influence [MATH] through the overall unitary. Conversely, if a unitary satisfies a number of no-influence conditions, it is natural to wonder whether a circuit decomposition exists in which all of them are represented by absences of paths. Such decompositions are known as causal decompositions; determining their existence in general is a central open problem in the study of causal structure in quantum theory. We present progress towards a general solution by considering the special case of unitary causal decompositions, i.e. decompositions in terms of unitary circuits in the traditional quantum circuit formalism that do not require the generalisation to 'extended' or 'routed' quantum circuits prompted by earlier research on this topic. We identify a combinatorial condition that characterises precisely those sets of no-influence constraints [MATH] for which any unitary transformation satisfying [MATH] admits a unitary causal decomposition representing the constraints. Our approach is systematic, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, and offers hope for extensions to more general (e.g. routed unitary) causal decompositions in the future.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes when sets of no-influence constraints on a unitary transformation admit a unitary causal decomposition, using lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra.
motivation: Causal decompositions are central to understanding causal structure in quantum theory, but determining their existence in general is a major open problem; this work makes progress by focusing on the special case of unitary causal decompositions.
method: The authors identify a combinatorial condition, grounded in lattice theory and finite-dimensional operator algebra, that precisely characterizes those no-influence constraint sets for which every satisfying unitary admits a unitary causal decomposition.
result: They obtain an exact characterization of unitary causal decomposability in terms of a combinatorial lattice-theoretic condition, without needing extended or routed quantum circuits.
conclusion: This provides systematic progress toward a general solution of causal decomposability and suggests a path toward extending the results to routed unitary causal decompositions.

title: Performance Of The Spin Qubit Shuttling Architecture For A Surface Code Implementation
authors: Berat Yenilen, Arnau Sala, Hendrik Bluhm, Markus Müller, And Manuel Rispler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2219 (2026).

Qubit shuttling promises to advance some quantum computing platforms to the qubit register sizes needed for effective quantum error correction (QEC), but also introduces additional errors whose impact must be evaluated. The established method to investigate the performance of QEC codes in a realistic scenario is to employ a standard noise model known as circuit-level noise, where all quantum operations are modeled as noisy. In the present work, we take this noise model and single out the effect of shuttling errors by introducing them as an additional so-called error location. This hardware abstraction is motivated by the SpinBus architecture and allows a systematic numerical investigation to map out the resulting two-dimensional parameter space. To this end, we take the Surface code and perform large scale simulations, most notably extracting the threshold across said two-dimensional parameter space. We study two scenarios for shuttling errors, depolarization on the one hand and dephasing on the other hand. For a purely dephasing shuttling error, we find a threshold of several percent, provided that all other operations have a high fidelity. The qubit overhead needed to reach a logical error rate of [MATH] (known as the "teraquop" regime [23] increases only moderately for shuttling error rates up to about 1 % per shuttling operation. The error rates at which practically useful, i.e. well below threshold error correction is predicted to be possible are comfortably higher than what is expected to be achievable for spin qubits. Our results thus show that it is reasonable to expect shuttling operations to fall below threshold already at surprisingly large error rates. With realistic efforts in the near term, this offers positive prospects for spin qubit based quantum processors as a viable avenue for scalable fault-tolerant error-corrected quantum computing.

.
tldr: This paper evaluates how spin-qubit shuttling errors affect the threshold and overhead of surface-code quantum error correction.
motivation: Qubit shuttling could enable scalable spin-qubit registers, but its added noise must be quantified for fault-tolerant quantum error correction.
method: The authors extend circuit-level noise models with shuttling error locations motivated by the SpinBus architecture and perform large-scale surface-code simulations over a two-dimensional parameter space for depolarizing and dephasing shuttling errors.
result: For purely dephasing shuttling errors, they find thresholds of several percent when other operations are high fidelity, and the qubit overhead to reach the teraquop regime grows only moderately up to about 1% shuttling error per operation.
conclusion: The expected spin-qubit shuttling error rates appear comfortably below threshold, supporting spin-qubit architectures as a viable route to scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Gibbs State Preparation For Commuting Hamiltonian: Mapping To Classical Gibbs Sampling
authors: Yeongwoo Hwang And Jiaqing Jiang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2209 (2026).

Gibbs state preparation, or Gibbs sampling, is a key computational technique extensively used in physics, statistics, and other scientific fields. Recent efforts for designing fast mixing Gibbs samplers for quantum Hamiltonians have largely focused on commuting local Hamiltonians (CLHs), a non-trivial subclass of Hamiltonians which include highly entangled systems such as the Toric code and quantum double model. Most previous Gibbs samplers relied on simulating the Davies generator, which is a Lindbladian associated with the thermalization process in nature. Instead of using the Davies generator, we design a different Gibbs sampler for various CLHs by giving a reduction to classical Hamiltonians, in the sense that one can efficiently prepare the Gibbs state for some CLH [MATH] on a quantum computer as long as one can efficiently do classical Gibbs sampling for the corresponding classical Hamiltonian [MATH]. We demonstrate that our Gibbs sampler is able to replicate state-of-the-art results as well as prepare the Gibbs state in regimes which were previously unknown, such as the low temperature region, as long as there exists fast mixing Gibbs samplers for the corresponding classical Hamiltonians. Our reductions are as follows. – If [MATH] is a 2-local qudit CLH, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are no classical qubits, then [MATH] is a 2-local qudit classical Hamiltonian on a planar graph. As an example, our algorithm can prepare the Gibbs state for the (defected) Toric code at any non-zero temperature in [MATH] time. – If [MATH] is a 4-local qubit CLH on 2D lattice and there are classical qubits, assuming that quantum terms are uniformly correctable, then [MATH] is a constant-local classical Hamiltonian.

.
tldr: The paper reduces quantum Gibbs state preparation for commuting local Hamiltonians to classical Gibbs sampling, enabling efficient thermal-state preparation in previously inaccessible regimes.
motivation: Fast-mixing quantum Gibbs samplers for commuting local Hamiltonians have largely relied on simulating the Davies generator, so the authors seek an alternative route based on classical Gibbs sampling.
method: They design reductions from commuting quantum Hamiltonians to classical Hamiltonians for several classes, including 2-local qudit CLHs and 4-local qubit CLHs on 2D lattices, then prepare the quantum Gibbs state via classical Gibbs sampling.
result: The sampler recovers state-of-the-art guarantees and can prepare Gibbs states at low temperature, including the defected Toric code at any nonzero temperature in polynomial time assuming fast mixing of the corresponding classical sampler.
conclusion: The work bridges quantum Gibbs state preparation and classical Gibbs sampling, extending efficient thermal-state preparation to new Hamiltonian classes and temperature regimes.

title: Multi-echo Evaluation Of Non-invertible Errors In Target Quantum Computations
authors: Ivan Henao And Raam Uzdin Jader P Santos
abstract: This work introduces a method for quantifying errors in quantum computations using multiple echoes of a target circuit. Our approach addresses a gap in the range of available benchmarking methods: unlike existing approaches that evaluate the average performance of a device, circuit, or gate, our method estimates the error in a target computation using the same initial state and circuit as the computation itself. It therefore captures how noise manifests in the specific computation of interest. We present two variants of the approach. The first estimates incoherent errors through purity loss, while the second estimates the echo infidelity, which captures both incoherent errors and non-invertible coherent errors, such as crosstalk. The purity-loss method applies to low-error circuits, or layers of gates, regardless of system size. The echo-infidelity method applies to circuits of arbitrary size and remains effective even at high error rates. Because our approach does not rely on an explicit noise model, it can complement methods that provide more detailed error information by testing the validity of the sparsity assumptions underlying those models. Finally, we discuss platforms on which our method can be implemented immediately.
tldr: The paper introduces multi-echo benchmarking protocols to estimate errors in a specific target quantum computation using the same initial state and circuit.
motivation: Existing benchmarking methods typically characterize average device, gate, or circuit performance rather than the error affecting a particular computation of interest.
method: Two variants are proposed: a purity-loss method for incoherent errors in low-error circuits or gate layers, and an echo-infidelity method that captures both incoherent and non-invertible coherent errors such as crosstalk.
result: The purity-loss approach works for low-error circuits regardless of system size, while the echo-infidelity approach applies to arbitrary-size circuits and remains effective at high error rates without relying on an explicit noise model.
conclusion: The method complements model-based error characterization by testing sparsity assumptions and can be implemented on existing quantum platforms.

title: Approach To Optimal Quantum Transport Via States Over Time
authors: Matt Hoogsteder-Riera, John Calsamiglia, And Andreas Winter
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2236 (2026).

We approach the problem of constructing a quantum analogue of the immensely fruitful classical transport cost theory of Monge from a new angle. Going back to the original motivations, by which the transport is a bilinear function of a mass distribution (without loss of generality a probability density) and a transport plan (a stochastic kernel), we explore the quantum version where the mass distribution is generalised to a density matrix, and the transport plan to a completely positive and trace preserving map. These two data are naturally integrated into their Jordan product, which is called state over time (“stote''), and the transport cost is postulated to be a linear function of it. We explore the properties of this transport cost, as well as the optimal transport cost between two given states (simply the minimum cost over all suitable transport plans). After that, we analyse in considerable detail the case of unitary invariant cost, for which we can calculate many costs analytically. These findings suggest that our quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from Monge's classical transport.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a quantum analogue of Monge transport cost by combining density matrices and CPTP maps through their Jordan product into a 'state over time' and analyzing the resulting optimal transport problem.
motivation: Classical Monge transport cost theory is highly fruitful, and the authors aim to construct a quantum counterpart using the original bilinear formulation of mass distribution and transport plan.
method: They generalize the mass distribution to a density matrix and the transport plan to a completely positive trace-preserving map, integrate them via the Jordan product, postulate a linear transport cost, and study its properties and optimal value.
result: They derive properties of the quantum transport cost and compute many costs analytically for unitary-invariant costs, finding that the quantum transport cost is qualitatively different from the classical Monge cost.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a mathematically rich quantum optimal transport cost whose behavior departs from classical transport, suggesting new directions in quantum information theory.

title: Universality Classes, Thermodynamics Of Group Entropies, And Black Holes
authors: Petr Jizba And Piergiulio Tempesta Henrik Jeldtoft Jensen
abstract: Conventional Boltzmann–Gibbs statistical mechanics successfully describes systems with weak to moderate correlations, in which the number of accessible configurations grows exponentially with the number of degrees of freedom . However, this framework breaks down for systems for which the effectively occupied configuration space exhibits non-exponential growth. While numerous generalized entropies have been proposed to address this limitation, a coherent link to classical thermodynamic laws has remained elusive. Here, we propose group entropies as a unifying framework, defining universality classes of entropies through the asymptotic scaling of , each yielding an extensive entropy. We show that this approach provides the basis for a consistent thermodynamic formulation beyond the Boltzmann–Gibbs paradigm. In particular, by expressing these entropies in terms of thermodynamic state variables, we demonstrate their consistency with classical thermodynamics, in close analogy to the emergence of the Clausius entropy from the Boltzmann–Gibbs formalism. Focusing on the zeroth thermodynamic law, we identify the empirical temperature and, by using Carathéodory’s formulation of the second law, we derive the associated absolute temperature. As an application, we analyse black-hole thermodynamics using the extensive group entropy class corresponding to stretched-exponential behaviour of and derive a negative heat capacity, known to be a hallmark property of black holes. This result holds for the stretched-exponential entropies associated with both the Bekenstein–Hawking and Barrow entropy scalings.
tldr: The paper introduces group entropies as a unifying framework for generalized statistical mechanics and derives consistent thermodynamic laws, applying the formalism to black-hole thermodynamics.
motivation: Boltzmann–Gibbs statistical mechanics fails for systems with non-exponential configuration-space growth, and existing generalized entropies lack a coherent link to classical thermodynamic laws.
method: The authors define universality classes of extensive group entropies via asymptotic scaling, express them in thermodynamic state variables, and use the zeroth law plus Carathéodory's second-law formulation to derive empirical and absolute temperatures.
result: The framework yields a consistent thermodynamic formulation beyond Boltzmann–Gibbs; for stretched-exponential group entropies applied to black holes, it produces a negative heat capacity for both Bekenstein–Hawking and Barrow entropy scalings.
conclusion: Group entropies provide a principled route to generalized thermodynamics, with black-hole thermodynamics as a concrete application, though the work is primarily classical/foundational rather than quantum-information-theoretic.

title: Rare Event Simulation Of Quantum Error-Correcting Circuits
authors: Carolyn Mayer, Anand Ganti, Uzoma Onunkwo, Tzvetan Metodi, Benjamin Anker, And Jacek Skryzalin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2237 (2026).

We describe a practical approach for accessing the logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting (QEC) circuits under low physical (component) failure rate regimes. Standard Monte Carlo is often the de facto approach for studying the failure rates of quantum circuits. However, in the study of fault-tolerant error-correcting circuits, the ability to extend this approach to low physical failure rates is limited. In particular, the use of Monte Carlo to access circuits that are relatively large or have high correcting power becomes more difficult as we lower the input failure rates of the individual components (gates) in the circuit. For these reasons, many simulations studying the circuit model go no lower than end-to-end logical failure rates in the [MATH] regime. In this report, we outline an approach that borrows from earlier work by Bravyi and Vargo [6] to the more complex circuit noise model. Earlier works studied both the capacity and phenomenological noise models [6,3,5], but the work is insufficient for generating similar simulations in the circuit-noise model. To the best of our knowledge, our team is the first to develop a full prescription of the rare event simulation by splitting technique for the circuit-based noise model. We have also generated promising results that are confirmed by standard Monte Carlo simulation under an accessible regime. This work shows that we can access noise in the circuit-model prescription of quantum error-correcting code to failure rates below [MATH] regime.

.
tldr: The paper develops a rare-event simulation method based on splitting to estimate logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting circuits under circuit-level noise at very low physical error rates.
motivation: Standard Monte Carlo simulation becomes impractical for estimating low logical failure rates in fault-tolerant QEC circuits, especially for large circuits or high-distance codes, limiting access to realistic low-noise regimes.
method: The authors adapt Bravyi-Vargo-style rare-event simulation via splitting to the circuit-noise model, providing a full prescription for QEC circuit failure-rate estimation and validating results against standard Monte Carlo in an accessible regime.
result: The approach accesses logical failure rates in the circuit-noise model below regimes typically reachable by Monte Carlo, with promising results confirmed by standard Monte Carlo where comparison is feasible.
conclusion: Rare-event simulation by splitting is a practical tool for characterizing QEC circuit performance at low physical failure rates and can extend fault-tolerance studies beyond conventional Monte Carlo limits.

title: Quantum Walks On Arbitrary Spatial Networks With Rydberg Atoms
authors: Gabriel Almeida, Raul Santos, Lara Janiurek, And Yasser Omar
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2235 (2026).

Rydberg atoms provide a highly promising platform for quantum computation, leveraging their strong tunable interactions to encode and manipulate information in the electronic states of individual atoms. Key advantages of Rydberg atoms include scalability, reconfigurable connectivity, and native multi-qubit gates, making them particularly well-suited for addressing complex network problems. These problems can often be framed as graph-based tasks, which can be efficiently addressed using quantum walks. In this work, we propose a general implementation of staggered quantum walks with Rydberg atoms, with a particular focus on spatial networks. We also present an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations required for the staggered quantum walk. Finally, we demonstrate that our proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup in spatial search algorithms.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a general Rydberg-atom implementation of staggered quantum walks on arbitrary spatial networks, including an efficient tessellation-construction algorithm and evidence of quadratic spatial-search speedup.
motivation: Rydberg atoms offer scalable, reconfigurable connectivity and native multi-qubit gates, making them promising for graph-based quantum information tasks, but general implementations of staggered quantum walks on spatial networks are lacking.
method: The authors map staggered quantum walks onto Rydberg-atom arrays and develop an efficient algorithm for constructing the tessellations required by the walk evolution, then analyze the resulting spatial-search performance.
result: The proposal achieves performance consistent with a quadratic speedup for spatial search and provides an efficient method for building the needed tessellations.
conclusion: Rydberg-atom platforms are viable for implementing network-based quantum walk algorithms, enabling graph-structured quantum search and related tasks.

title: Enhanced Measurements On Quantum Computers Via The Simultaneous Probing Of Non-commuting Pauli Operators
authors: Rick P. A. Simon, Zheng Shi, Charlie Nation, Andrew Jena, And Luca Dellantonio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2229 (2026).

Measuring the state of quantum computers is a highly non-trivial task, with implications for virtually all quantum algorithms. A promising avenue is multi-copy schemes, where identical copies of a quantum state are measured jointly so that all Pauli operators within the considered observable can be simultaneously assessed. Here, we present a first implementation of such a two-copy scheme in a measurement protocol. Based on Bayesian statistics, it accurately estimates not only the average of the desired observable but also the error en route. This enables an adaptive shot-allocation algorithm that preferentially samples the most uncertain Pauli terms. In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, this “double'' scheme can outperform the state-of-the-art measurement protocol in minimizing total shots for a given precision. We also numerically confirm the finding in previous theoretical works that the two-copy scheme incurs an overhead due to the square-root relationship between the variance of measured quantities and the number of measurement shots.

.
tldr: The paper implements a two-copy Bayesian measurement protocol that jointly estimates non-commuting Pauli operators on quantum computers with adaptive shot allocation.
motivation: Measuring observables on quantum computers is costly, especially when many Pauli terms are non-commuting, so multi-copy joint measurements may reduce the number of shots needed for a target precision.
method: The authors realize a two-copy scheme in which identical state copies are measured jointly, use Bayesian statistics to estimate the observable mean and error, and adaptively allocate shots to the most uncertain Pauli terms.
result: In regimes with many non-commuting Pauli operators, the double scheme can outperform state-of-the-art measurement protocols in minimizing total shots, while numerical results confirm a square-root variance overhead from two-copy measurements.
conclusion: Two-copy adaptive Bayesian measurement is a promising practical approach for observable estimation on quantum computers, though its advantage is regime-dependent and carries an overhead.

title: Compound Beams For Direct Experimental Comparison Of Quantum Operations
authors: Kishore Thapliyal, Jan Peřina Jr, Pavel Pavlíček And Antonín Černoch
abstract: Compound beams composed of simple experimental blocks (detected in simultaneous detection windows) that form specific quantum-correlated structures are suggested for simulating the properties of different quantum operations used for creating highly nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states needed in quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols. Qualitative and quantitative comparison of multi-photon addition (PA) and subtraction in compound multi-mode thermal as well as sub-Poissonian beams and multi-mode twin beams with their intensities extending over two orders in magnitude is provided. Adding and subtracting up to twenty photocounts, optimal conditions for the generation of experimental nonclassical states are identified. In general, PA is identified as advantageous over photon subtraction (PS) for the multi-mode thermal and sub-Poissonian beams: It induces (enhances) the nonclassicality in the former (latter) state. Contrary to this, PS outperforms PA in the multi-mode twin beams. Moreover, exploiting temporal photon-pair correlations in compound twin beams when post-selecting, nearly ideal experimental photon(s) addition is demonstrated. The results apply for the beams with mean photon number per mode much less than one.
tldr: The paper experimentally compares multi-photon addition and subtraction in compound multi-mode thermal, sub-Poissonian, and twin beams for generating nonclassical states.
motivation: Photon addition and subtraction are important operations for preparing nonclassical and entangled multi-mode states used in quantum communication, metrology, and information protocols, but direct experimental comparisons across beam types are needed.
method: Compound beams composed of simple experimental blocks are used to simulate and compare multi-photon addition and subtraction up to twenty photocounts in multi-mode thermal, sub-Poissonian, and twin beams over a wide intensity range.
result: Photon addition is generally advantageous for multi-mode thermal and sub-Poissonian beams, inducing or enhancing nonclassicality, while photon subtraction outperforms addition in multi-mode twin beams; post-selection on temporal photon-pair correlations enables nearly ideal photon addition.
conclusion: The work identifies optimal conditions for generating experimental nonclassical states via photon addition and subtraction, with results applicable when the mean photon number per mode is much less than one.

title: Spinor Bose-Einstein Condensate As An Analog Simulator Of Molecular Bending Vibrations
authors: Ayaka Usui, Artur Niezgoda, And Manuel Gessner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2226 (2026).

We demonstrate that spinor Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) can be operated as an analog simulator of the two-dimensional vibron model. This algebraic model describes bending vibrations of molecules and, in the case of triatomic molecules, exhibits two phases where linear and bent configurations are stabilised. Spinor BECs can be engineered to simulate states that correspond to linear or bent triatomic molecules, with the Wigner function of the BEC encoding information about the molecular configuration. We show how quantum simulations of the bending dynamics of linear molecules can be realised, and how preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase leads to a dynamical instability. In the dynamics triggered by the corresponding instability, a significant amount of entanglement is generated, and we characterise the dynamics with the squeezing parameter and the quantum Fisher information (QFI). The scaling of the non-Gaussian sensitivity, described by the difference between squeezing and QFI, grows with the system size once the spinor system crosses from the linear to the bent phase, thus serving as a dynamical witness for the quantum phase transition.

.
tldr: The paper shows that spinor BECs can simulate the two-dimensional vibron model of molecular bending vibrations, with entanglement and QFI witnessing a dynamical instability across linear-to-bent phases.
motivation: Molecular bending vibrations are described by algebraic vibron models with linear and bent configurations; the authors seek a controllable quantum platform to simulate this dynamics and probe nonclassical features.
method: They engineer a spinor BEC to represent the two-dimensional vibron model, encode molecular configuration in the BEC Wigner function, and analyze quench dynamics triggered by preparing a linear configuration in the bent phase using squeezing and quantum Fisher information.
result: The instability generates significant entanglement, and the non-Gaussian sensitivity, described by the difference between squeezing and QFI, scales with system size after crossing from the linear to the bent phase, acting as a dynamical witness of the quantum phase transition.
conclusion: Spinor BECs provide an analog simulator of molecular bending dynamics and a route to study entanglement, non-Gaussian sensitivity, and phase transitions in a controllable atomic system.

title: Stability Of Majorana Zero Modes With Quantum Optical Lattices
authors: Santiago F Caballero-Benitez
abstract: I analyze the emergence of Majorana zero modes (MZM) in a one dimensional ultracold fermionic system confined by an optical lattice inside a high-Q cavity. This forms a quantum optical lattice due to the cavity backaction, with emergent long range interactions controlled by the light pumped into the system and thus long range pairing. I investigate the possibility of formation and emergence of edge modes using exact diagonalization with self-consistent order parameters and singular value decomposition of the Hamiltonian in the Majorana representation. I analyze the spectral properties of the system, the mass gap and amplitude of the MZM with a unified framework. The interplay of cavity induced interactions and effective -wave short range interactions controls the emergence of the signatures of MZM. I find that under certain conditions MZM distinctively emerge leading to superradiant topological phases of matter. These MZM have potential applications for quantum information as they are topologically protected analogous to the behavior of the Kitaev chain. The techniques employed lead to a scheme based on the Majorana representation and exact diagonalization with self consistent conditions using Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov theory in real space for finite systems that can be applied to other fermionic and analog systems termed Light-Matter-Majorana. A promising landscape for the exploration of short range and long range topological order with superradiance is found.
tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes the emergence and stability of Majorana zero modes in a one-dimensional ultracold fermionic gas confined by an optical lattice inside a high-Q cavity.
motivation: Majorana zero modes are topologically protected excitations with potential quantum-information applications, and the authors aim to explore whether cavity-induced long-range interactions can stabilize them in a cold-atom platform.
method: The author uses exact diagonalization with self-consistent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov order parameters and singular value decomposition in the Majorana representation to study finite-size spectral properties, mass gaps, and edge-mode amplitudes.
result: Under suitable interplay between cavity-induced long-range interactions and short-range p-wave interactions, distinct Majorana zero modes emerge, enabling superradiant topological phases of matter.
conclusion: The work proposes a light-matter Majorana framework for exploring topological order with superradiance in quantum optical lattices, with potential relevance to topological quantum information.

title: Universal Dilation Of Linear Itô SDEs: Quantum Trajectories And Lindblad Simulation Of Second Moments
authors: Hsuan-Cheng Wu And Xiantao Li
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2223 (2026).

We present a universal framework for simulating [MATH]-dimensional linear Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on quantum computers with additive or multiplicative noises. Building on a unitary dilation technique, we establish a rigorous mapping from the general linear SDEs [MATH] to stochastic Schrödinger equations (SSE) on a dilated Hilbert space. Crucially, this embedding is pathwise exact in that the classical solution is recovered as a projection of the dilated quantum state for each fixed noise realization. We demonstrate that the resulting SSEs are naturally implementable on digital quantum processors, where the stochastic Wiener increments are encoded directly by preparing the ancillary qubits. Exploiting this physical mapping, we develop two algorithmic strategies: (1) a trajectory-based approach that uses sequential weak measurements to realize efficient stochastic integrators, including a second-order scheme, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a deterministic Lindblad quantum master equation, enabling simulation without Monte Carlo sampling. We provide error bounds based on a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework with numerical experiments.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a unitary-dilation framework for simulating linear Itô SDEs on quantum computers via stochastic Schrödinger equations and Lindblad dynamics for second moments.
motivation: Classical stochastic differential equations are central to modeling noisy dynamics, but simulating them efficiently on quantum hardware requires a rigorous mapping to unitary quantum dynamics.
method: The authors construct a pathwise-exact unitary dilation that embeds linear Itô SDEs into stochastic Schrödinger equations on a dilated Hilbert space, implement the Wiener increments via ancilla preparation, and develop both trajectory-based weak-measurement integrators and an ensemble Lindblad master-equation approach.
result: They provide error bounds from a stochastic light-cone analysis, obtain a second-order stochastic integrator, and validate the framework numerically; the ensemble approach simulates moment evolution deterministically without Monte Carlo sampling.
conclusion: The work offers a universal quantum simulation framework for linear SDEs and their second moments, with potential relevance to open quantum system and stochastic dynamics modeling.

title: Quantum Fisher Information And Photon Statistics From Shift Current Shot Noise
authors: Evgenii Bartstakahiro Morimotonaoto Nagaosaahttps://ror.org/03gv2xk61riken Center For Emergent Matter Science, Wako 351-0198, Saitama, Japanbhttps://ror.org/057zh3y96department Of Applied Physics, The University Of Tokyo, Hongo 113-8656, Tokyo, Japancfundamental Quantum Science Program, Transformative Research Innovation Platform Headquarters, RIKEN, Wako 351-0198, Japan
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 41, October 2026.
SignificanceQuantum states of light carry useful information in their fluctuations, but converting those fluctuations into an electrical signal remains difficult. We identify a distinct route based on shift current: a local change in polarization in a ...
tldr: The paper proposes using shift-current shot noise to extract photon statistics and quantum Fisher information from quantum fluctuations of light.
motivation: Quantum states of light encode useful information in their fluctuations, but converting these optical fluctuations into an electrical signal remains experimentally difficult.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the shot noise of shift current—a local polarization change—and connect it to photon statistics and quantum Fisher information.
result: They identify a distinct route by which shift-current shot noise can reveal photon statistics and provide access to quantum Fisher information.
conclusion: Shift current may serve as an electrical probe of quantum optical fluctuations, with potential relevance for photodetection and quantum estimation.

title: Heuristic And Optimal Synthesis Of Cnot And Clifford Circuits
authors: Mark Webster, Stergios Koutsioumpas, And Dan E Browne
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2212 (2026).

Efficiently implementing Clifford circuits is crucial for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms. Linear reversible circuits, equivalent to circuits composed of CNOT\xspace gates, have important applications in classical computing. In this work we present methods for CNOT\xspace and general Clifford circuit synthesis which can be used to minimise either the entangling two-qubit gate count or the circuit depth. We present three families of algorithms - optimal synthesis which works on small circuits, A* synthesis for intermediate-size circuits and greedy synthesis for large circuits. We benchmark against existing methods, including rustiq, tket and qiskit and show that our approach results in circuits with lower two-qubit gate count. For encoding circuits, our methods outperform previous reinforcement learning results and find a lower two-qubit gate count circuit for the Golay code than previously known. The algorithms have been implemented in a GitHub repository for use by the classical and quantum computing community.

GitHub Repository

.
tldr: The paper introduces optimal, A*, and greedy algorithms for synthesizing CNOT and Clifford circuits while minimizing two-qubit gate count or circuit depth.
motivation: Efficient Clifford and CNOT circuit synthesis is important for quantum error correction and quantum algorithms, but existing synthesis methods can produce suboptimal circuits.
method: The authors develop three algorithm families for small, intermediate, and large circuits and benchmark them against rustiq, tket, and qiskit, including encoding-circuit applications.
result: Their methods achieve lower two-qubit gate counts than existing tools, outperform previous reinforcement-learning results for encoding circuits, and find a lower-gate-count circuit for the Golay code.
conclusion: The work provides practical circuit-synthesis tools for the classical and quantum computing communities, with implementations released on GitHub.

title: Quantum Algorithms For General Nonlinear Dynamics Based On The Carleman Embedding
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Andrew T Sornborger, Yigit Subasi, And Guoming Wang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2233 (2026).

Important nonlinear dynamics, such as those found in plasma and fluid systems, are typically hard to simulate on classical computers. Thus, if fault-tolerant quantum computers could efficiently solve such nonlinear problems, it would be a transformative change for many industries. In a recent breakthrough [Liu et al., PNAS 2021], the first efficient quantum algorithm for solving nonlinear differential equations was constructed, based on a single condition [MATH], where [MATH] characterizes the ratio of nonlinearity to dissipation. This result, however, is limited to the class of purely dissipative systems with negative log-norm, which excludes application to many important problems. In this work, we correct technical issues with this and other prior analysis, and substantially extend the scope of nonlinear dynamical systems that can be efficiently simulated on a quantum computer in a number of ways. Firstly, we extend the existing results from purely dissipative systems to a much broader class of stable systems, and show that every quadratic Lyapunov function for the linearized system corresponds to an independent [MATH]-number criterion for the convergence of the Carleman scheme. Secondly, we extend our stable system results to physically relevant settings where conserved polynomial quantities exist. Finally, we provide extensive results for the class of non-resonant systems. With this, we are able to show that efficient quantum algorithms exist for a much wider class of nonlinear systems than previously known, and prove the BQP-completeness of nonlinear oscillator problems of exponential size. In our analysis, we also obtain several results related to the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and diagonalization of the Carleman matrix, which could be of independent interest.

.
tldr: This paper develops quantum algorithms for simulating a broad class of nonlinear dynamical systems using the Carleman embedding and establishes BQP-completeness for certain nonlinear oscillator problems.
motivation: Many important nonlinear dynamics are hard to simulate classically, and prior quantum algorithms based on the Carleman embedding were limited to purely dissipative systems with restrictive convergence criteria.
method: The authors correct prior technical analyses and extend Carleman-embedding-based quantum algorithms to broader stable systems using quadratic Lyapunov functions, conserved polynomial quantities, and non-resonant conditions, with additional results on the Poincaré-Dulac theorem and Carleman matrix diagonalization.
result: They show efficient quantum algorithms exist for a much wider class of nonlinear systems than previously known and prove BQP-completeness for exponentially large nonlinear oscillator problems.
conclusion: The work significantly broadens the applicability of quantum algorithms for nonlinear dynamics, though its primary contribution is in quantum algorithms and complexity rather than the researcher's core quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems interests.

title: Order Parameter Discovery For Quantum Many-Body Systems
authors: Nicola Mariella, Tara Murphy, Francesco Di Marcantonio, Khadijeh Najafi, Sofia Vallecorsa, Sergiy Zhuk, And Enrique Rico
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2217 (2026).

Quantum phase transitions reveal deep insights into the behavior of many-body quantum systems, but identifying these transitions without prior knowledge of order parameters remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce a method for constructing phase diagrams using the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility (RFS), and demonstrate how information encoded in this vector field can be used to discover observables corresponding to order parameters. We apply our approach to well-established models: the Axial Next Nearest Neighbour Interaction (ANNNI) model, a cluster state model, and a chain of Rydberg atoms; and validate the discovered order parameters using eigendecomposition and finite-size scaling analysis, confirming the expected universality classes. Our results demonstrate that the RFS vector field offers a unified framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery that requires no prior knowledge of symmetry or transition type, while relying only on reduced density matrices of small subsystems.

.
tldr: The authors propose a method to construct quantum phase diagrams and discover order parameters from the vector field of the reduced fidelity susceptibility, requiring only small-subsystem reduced density matrices.
motivation: Identifying quantum phase transitions typically requires prior knowledge of the relevant order parameter or symmetry, which is often unavailable for poorly understood many-body models.
method: They build a vector field from the reduced fidelity susceptibility computed from reduced density matrices of small subsystems, then construct phase diagrams and extract candidate order-parameter observables from the field's structure, validating them via eigendecomposition and finite-size scaling.
result: The approach recovers known order parameters and universality classes for the ANNNI model, a cluster-state model, and a Rydberg-atom chain without prior symmetry or transition-type knowledge.
conclusion: The RFS vector field provides a unified, assumption-light framework for phase characterization and order-parameter discovery in quantum many-body systems.

title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Simulation Of Stabilizer Circuits
authors: Muhammad Osama, Dimitrios Thanos, And Alfons Laarman
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2225 (2026).

We introduce new parallel algorithms for efficiently simulating stabilizer (Clifford) circuits on GPUs, with a focus on data-parallel tableau evolution and scalable handling of projective measurements. Our approach reformulates key bottlenecks in stabilizer simulation – such as Gaussian elimination and measurement updates – into GPU-tailored primitives that eliminate sequential dependencies and maximize memory coalescing. We implement these techniques in QuaSARQ, a GPU-accelerated stabilizer simulator designed for large qubit counts and many-shot sampling. Across a broad benchmark suite reaching 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000 (roughly 130M gates), QuaSARQ shows substantial runtime improvements, with up to 105[MATH] speedup, and over 80% energy reduction on demanding instances. Moreover, QuaSARQ consistently outperforms Stim, a state-of-the-art CPU-optimized stabilizer simulator, as well as Qiskit-Aer (CPU/GPU), Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane. Finally, QuaSARQ exhibits a significant advantage in many-shot sampling on large workloads. These results demonstrate that our parallel algorithms can significantly advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, particularly for workloads involving extensive measurements and sampling.

The open-source implementation of QuaSARQ is available at GitHub.

.
tldr: QuaSARQ is a GPU-accelerated stabilizer (Clifford) circuit simulator that parallelizes tableau evolution and projective measurement updates, achieving large speedups and energy savings over Stim and other simulators.
motivation: Simulating stabilizer circuits classically at large qubit counts and many shots is bottlenecked by sequential steps such as Gaussian elimination and measurement updates; the authors aim to remove these serial dependencies using GPU-friendly primitives.
method: The authors reformulate tableau evolution, Gaussian elimination, and measurement sampling into data-parallel, memory-coalesced GPU kernels, implemented in the open-source QuaSARQ simulator.
result: On benchmarks up to 180,000 qubits and depth 1,000 (~130M gates), QuaSARQ reports up to 105x speedup and over 80% energy reduction, outperforming Stim, Qiskit-Aer CPU/GPU, Qibo, Cirq, and PennyLane, with particular advantage in many-shot sampling.
conclusion: Parallel GPU algorithms substantially advance the scalability of stabilizer-circuit simulation, especially for measurement- and sampling-heavy workloads.

title: Evidence For Exceptional Points As Topological Defects
authors: Chia-Yi Ju And Szu-Ming Chen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2220 (2026).

Studies have shown that quantum states reside in a Hilbert space bundle. When a quantum system depends on continuous external parameters, these parameters define additional dimensions in the base space of the bundle. While much of the existing literature focuses on eigenstate subbundles, where geometric properties like Berry curvature arise, this work considers the entire Hilbert space bundle. Although the Hilbert space bundle has been found to be locally flat, suggesting that the system's topology may appear trivial, we revisit this assumption. Specifically, we examine how an arbitrary quantum state evolves when transported along closed parameter loops, a phenomenon characterized by holonomy. Our results demonstrate that nontrivial holonomy can emerge in the presence of exceptional points. Consequently, exceptional points naturally manifest as topological defects. Finally, we show that this nontrivial topology manifests in physical, time-dependent evolutions, providing a simple experimental signature to detect exceptional points by comparing state transport along distinct paths.

.
tldr: The paper shows that nontrivial holonomy of the full Hilbert space bundle arises around exceptional points, making them topological defects with an experimentally detectable signature.
motivation: Existing literature on geometric phases focuses on eigenstate subbundles, while the full Hilbert space bundle is often taken to be locally flat and hence topologically trivial; the authors revisit whether genuine topology can still appear.
method: They analyze holonomy of arbitrary quantum states transported along closed loops in parameter space, using the bundle structure of Hilbert space in the presence of exceptional points, and propose time-dependent evolution protocols to probe the effect.
result: Nontrivial holonomy emerges when loops enclose exceptional points, so exceptional points act as topological defects; the topology leaves a signature in physical time-dependent dynamics.
conclusion: Exceptional points can be detected by comparing state transport along distinct paths, offering a simple experimental test grounded in the global topology of the Hilbert space bundle.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: The paper presents a circuit-construction method for preparing sparse quantum states with reduced Toffoli-gate cost via an efficient isometry implementation.
motivation: Sparse state preparation is a key primitive for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers, and reducing its gate cost is important for practical quantum algorithms.
method: The authors prepare a dense state on a small sub-register and then map it to the target sparse state using an isometry, designing a batched and optimized isometry circuit.
result: The worst-case Toffoli cost is essentially quadratic for sufficiently large sparsity, giving roughly a square-root improvement over prior art; numerical benchmarks show even lower costs.
conclusion: The improved isometry circuit reduces the cost of sparse state preparation and allows joint optimization with the dense-state preparation step, especially for real-amplitude target states.

title: Generalising Aumann’s Agreement Theorem
authors: Matthew Leifer And Cristhiano Duarte
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2210 (2026).

According to Aumann's celebrated theorem, rational agents cannot agree to disagree. In other words, agents who once shared a common prior probability distribution and who have common knowledge about their posteriors cannot assign different probability distributions to a given proposition. Common knowledge imposes strong restrictions on assigned probabilities. In fact, Aumann's agreement theorem was one of the first attempts to formalise and explore the role played by common knowledge in decision theory. Recently, the debate over possible (quantum) extensions of Aumann's results has resurfaced. This paper contributes to this discussion. First, we argue that agreeing to disagree is impossible in quantum theory. Secondly, by building on the quantum argument, we show that agreeing to disagree is also forbidden in any generalised probability theory. The upshot is that in its probabilistic version, the agreement theorem is a direct consequence of how we choose to condition upon acquiring new information.

.
tldr: The paper argues that rational agents cannot agree to disagree in quantum theory and, more generally, in any generalised probabilistic theory.
motivation: Aumann's agreement theorem is a foundational result about common knowledge and posterior probabilities, and recent work has revisited whether it extends to quantum and generalised probabilistic settings.
method: The authors analyse the role of common knowledge and Bayesian conditioning in quantum theory, then abstract the argument to generalised probability theories.
result: They show that the impossibility of agreeing to disagree follows from how agents condition on new information, and thus holds beyond classical probability.
conclusion: In its probabilistic form, the agreement theorem is a consequence of the conditioning rule rather than a specifically classical or quantum feature.

title: Limits To Black-box Amplification In Qma
authors: Scott Aaronson, Phillip Harris, And Freek Witteveen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2227 (2026).

We study the limitations of black-box amplification in the quantum complexity class [MATH]. Amplification is known to boost any inverse-polynomial gap between completeness and soundness to exponentially small error, and a recent result (Jeffery and Witteveen, 2025) shows that completeness can in fact be amplified to be doubly exponentially close to 1. We prove that this is optimal for black-box procedures: we provide a quantum oracle relative to which no [MATH] verification procedure using polynomial resources can achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential, or a soundness which is super-exponentially small. This is proven by making the oracle separation from (Aaronson, 2009) between [MATH] and [MATH] quantitative, using techniques from complex approximation theory.

.
tldr: The paper establishes tight limits on black-box amplification in QMA, showing that doubly-exponential completeness and super-exponentially small soundness are optimal relative to a quantum oracle.
motivation: Amplification of completeness/soundness gaps is fundamental to the robustness of quantum complexity classes, and a recent result showed completeness can be amplified to doubly exponentially close to 1; it was unclear whether this bound is optimal for black-box procedures.
method: The authors construct a quantum oracle, quantitatively strengthening the earlier QMA vs QMA(2)-style separation of Aaronson (2009), and use techniques from complex approximation theory to prove lower bounds on achievable completeness and soundness parameters.
result: They prove that no polynomial-resource QMA verification procedure can, relative to this oracle, achieve completeness closer to 1 than doubly exponential or soundness smaller than super-exponential, establishing optimality of known amplification procedures.
